newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan's press union urges caution after crackdown.
newsitem.headline: Jordan's press union urges caution after crackdown.

text.p: Jordan's press union has urged newspapers to curb salacious stories of sex and political intrigue after unprecendented jail terms passed this month on three journalists who ruffled conservative sensibilities.

Warning that they could provoke the government into draconian measures to increase control over the media, the Jordan Press Association told sensationalist weekly papers "not to tarnish our culture, values and tradition."
"Some papers have abused freedoms in a scandalous way, trampling over all morals," said the union statement, published in newspapers on Tuesday.
Three newspaper editors were sentenced to jail terms this month on charges including publishing slander and pornographic material.

All three were editors of privately-owned weekly newspapers. Some weeklies, unlike the staid, pro-government dailies, splash their front pages with scandals or political gossip. Others are mouthpieces for opposition groups.

"We are telling journalists to abide by ethical rules," said Seif Sherif, head of the union and director of the daily Ad-Dustour newspaper. But the jail terms, which he said were the first to be passed for publishing offences, showed "the reaction from the authorities was also tough."

Last week a court sentenced Abdullah bin Issa, editor of al-Hayat weekly, to six months in jail for publishing an interview in the now defunct al-Hiwar paper that it said propagated an outlawed Islamist party doctrine and slandered King Hussein.

Since then two more editors have been sentenced. The Jordan Times said Nael Salah, of the weekly al-Haqiqa, was given nine months in prison and ordered to pay 15,000 dinars ($21,200) for "spreading false news and publishing pornographic material".
Khalid Kassassbeh, former editor of al-Bilad now in the United States, was tried in absentia and sentenced to eight months in jail, his former colleagues said.
Lawyers representing journalists say dozens of charges are still outstanding.

Two editors at the satirical Abed Rebbo face charges for slandering a minister and labelling an Islamist parliamentarian a hypocrite for siding with pro-government deputies trying to shut down a television comedy which poked fun at parliament.
Another journalist was charged on Monday for an article about satanic practices in the town of Madaba, Sherif said.
Raja Talab, chief editor of the best-selling Shihan weekly, said there was a government campaign to put checks on the more free-wheeling press.
"If this campaign continues, in which some of the Islamic deputies and the government have joined forces, there will be a tightening of the grip on press freedom," he said.

Many independent weekly newspapers have been set up since Jordan lifted martial law in 1989. But with over 30 weeklies in a country of just four million people, some are struggling to get a circulation of over 2,000.
"Some of them are facing financial problems, but we tell them bluntly not just to follow the orders of their publishers who are trying to increase circulation," Sherif said.
